summary:
Emberwatch is an interactive wildfire monitoring and historical prediction platform designed to analyse satellite detected fire activity across Northern California using 2025 MODIS hotspot observations from NASA's FIRMS.

It divides Northern California into 10x10km grid cells and uses historical fire detections to rank areas according to their relative risk of experiencing newly detected fire activity within the following 24 hours.

During evaluation across 83 held-out days, our baseline model identified 21 of 59 newly detected fire-activity events within the highest risk 10% of eligible grid cells, achieving a recall of approximately 35.6%.

Emberwatch shows these rankings through interactive, colour coded wildfire map. Users can explore previous predictions, reveal subsequent satellite observations, and analyse historical fire activity across different time periods making satellite fire data easier to visualise, analyse and interpret.

It is still a prototype and it provides a foundation for multi sensor integration.
details:
EMBERWATCH. Detailed Project Description

What does our project do?

Emberwatch is an interactive wildfire monitoring and historical prediction platform designed to analyse satellite detected fire activity across Northern California using 2025 MODIS hotspot observations from NASA's FIRMS.

It divides Northern California into 10x10km grid cells and uses historical fire detections to rank areas according to their relative risk of experiencing newly detected fire activity within the following 24 hours.

During evaluation across 83 held-out days, our baseline model identified 21 of 59 newly detected fire-activity events within the highest risk 10% of eligible grid cells, achieving a recall of approximately 35.6%.

Emberwatch shows these rankings through interactive, colour coded wildfire map. Users can explore previous predictions, reveal subsequent satellite observations, and analyse historical fire activity across different time periods making satellite fire data easier to visualise, analyse and interpret.

How does EMBERWATCH work?

Our site allows you to browse the wildfire data via a map of Northern California. Each grid cell is coloured according to its relative risk ranking so the differences in fire activity are much more apparent.

Users can select cells to see the observations that went into the ranking.

An important feature is our replay system which allows the user to select a date and view the model's prediction for the 24 hours, then go on to see what the satellite actually detected. This is a much better way of understanding the model's accuracy and its limitations than just looking at the predictions with no evidence.

We've also added a fire activity calendar so users can look at the patterns over months and days.

What technologies did we use?

Emberwatch was a Python application for satellite data processing, geographical analysis and historical forecasting.

We're using FastAPI and Uvicorn for the backend, along with NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn and PyProj for the analysis, geospatial transformations and modelling.

The website interface was built using HTML, CSS and JavaScript with OpenStreetMap as the base for the map.

We published the source code via Github so that it could be inspected and further developed.

AI assisted development tools (including ChatGPT) were used to aid with coding, debugging, app development and visual aesthetics. However ideas and research were almost all independent from Ai

What makes our project creative?

An important element of Emberwatch is the combination of forecasting with model evaluation.

Just showing the satellite hotspot locations the platform enables you to see how the predictions are being made and to compare them with the actual observations.

Our historical replay feature helps make the forecasting process far more transparent and easier to understand (even when the forecast is wrong).

Another major element of our proposed development is the harmonisation of the MODIS and VIIRS satellite observations.

These instruments all have spatial resolution, detection sensitivity and observation time. The combination of their data therefore requires standardisation and methods to prevent double counting of the activity.

Although our current prototype is primarily using MODIS observations we've built a framework to support the integration and comparison of both sensors.

What factors did we consider?

We looked at the reliability of the satellite observations, the geographical resolution, the availability of the data and the potential for making misleading predictions.

We knew that satellite detected hotspots didn't necessarily equate to confirmed fires and that the absence of a detection didn't necessarily mean there wasn't a fire.

We also considered the importance of avoiding leakage in the testing of predictions. Our evaluation holds the observations from later testing periods so that the predictions are based on information that would have been available prior to the forecast window.

Given the development time we've had we've concentrated on producing a working prototype using the MODIS data set with a note that other improvements (addition of VIIRS data, weather data, improved predictive modelling etc) could be made.

What impact do we hope to achieve?

Our aim is to make satellite fire observations easier to access, easier to interpret and easier to compare.

By providing a platform to look at wildfire trends and the historical performance of the models EMBERWATCH could be of use in education, research and in increasing our understanding of wildfire activity in Northern California.

With development particularly around the integration of MODIS and VIIRS observations with the meteorological and environmental data the platform could be of use in research into wildfire monitoring and preparedness.

We hope EMBERWATCH demonstrates how readily available satellite observations, computational modelling and accessible visuals can be brought together to explore a key environmental issue.
